newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cyberspace copyrighters struggle at Geneva talks.
newsitem.headline: Cyberspace copyrighters struggle at Geneva talks.

text.p: Copyright experts determined to pin down piracy in the elusive cyberspace said on Thursday they first had to grapple with an unwieldy United Nations conference before getting down to the nitty-gritty of the digital agenda.

Inside a gloomy Geneva conference centre dubbed "the bunker", more than 800 copyright officials, diplomats and legislators have been locked up since December 2 to create a new roadmap for copyrights on the information superhighway.

A senior official of the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO), a U.N. agency which coordinates protection of copyrights and patents, said disputes were raging over proposals to update the century-old Berne copyright convention.
Informal talks in smaller groups were needed for progress.
"We can't debate these pacts with 800 people. We'll start informal consultations," he said, asking not to be named.
Informal talks will cut out nations with no views on how to tidy up the Internet, a global computer system likened to a giant copying machine which has ripped up copyright rulebooks.
In Geneva, many of the delegates from nations small and large, from Mongolia to Azerbaijan, have no Internet experience.
"I'd guess a third of the delegates have used a keyboard," said Alfons Schafers, deputy head of the German delegation. "But you don't have to be a murderer to write legislation on murder."

Officials said multi-billion-dollar industries and the world's nations remained deeply divided over a stack of proposals covering literary and artistic works, the rights of performers and producers of music and producers of databases.
The United States, the world's top intellectual property exporter, supports the pacts while developing nations with little interest in defending foreign copyrights oppose them.

Attempts by software, music and entertainment companies to ensure they get a cut from electronic works have created a furore in the online community, which says the pacts expose them to liability and give huge powers to copyright-based industries.
"There are so many conflicting interests between different countries, Internet providers and other industries," said Mihaly Ficsor, deputy-director general of WIPO.

Officials said it was still unclear after days of wrangling, for instance, if the treaties would exclude economically irrelevant copying such as innocent Web surfing -- which by definition requires that a computer make transient copies.
There was also no accord on digital rights for audiovisual performers and the legality of devices and decoders that allow users to pick electronic locks on copyrighted works.
Conference officials struggled to give a sense of consensus at a Wednesday night briefing but only added to the confusion.

"Who's responsible for infringement? The person who pressed the button? A person who asked someone else to press the button? Or the owner of an establishment where the button was pressed?" asked Jukka Liedes, a Finnish member of the steering committee.

"Who's responsible for pressing that button really has to be looked at closely," he said. "Internet is a global phenomenon and we have to define it. There is no global legislation. We have to conclude treaties which will govern national solutions."
Asked to clarify the confusion, he said: "I wrote these treaties. I understand them. I hope people who don't understand them consult some expert help."
